steps.text: This is enough evidence - it matches the simulated T1543.003 persistence technique, so I'll classify it as malicious and submit my verdict.

submission.reasoning: On workstation5, user wardog ran an interactive elevated cmd.exe (proc-690e6c933a). From it, sc.exe (proc-f4d3576242) changed the Fax service binPath to 'powershell.exe -noexit -c "write-host 'T1543.003 Test'"'. 'sc start Fax' (proc-cd222a569d) then started the service, and the Service Control Manager launched the PowerShell payload as NT AUTHORITY\NETWORK SERVICE (proc-7f9f3418e9). After that, 'sc config Fax binPath= fxssvc.exe' (proc-babd722e6c) put the original path back, and the Fax ImagePath registry value (reg-e3a6a6345f) now reads C:\WINDOWS\system32\fxssvc.exe again. This matches the MITRE T1543.003 technique (hijacking a Windows service to run code) and looks like an Atomic Red Team test. It is treated as malicious: a service was hijacked to run code under a service account, even though the change was later reverted.
